proof_skeleton_nl: Clear only the genuine denominator of the theorem sum by multiplying with E_{d,n}(q)=(q^{2d};q^{2d})_{n-1}; this gives a Laurent polynomial P_{d,r,n}(q). Factor the target modulus as [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2 = U_n(q) Φ_n(q)^3, where U_n(q) is the product of the cyclotomic polynomials Φ_m(q) for proper divisors m of n. Prove the U_n(q)-part by a theorem-specific vanishing lemma at primitive roots of proper divisors of n together with an abstract cyclotomic-divisibility criterion. Prove the Φ_n(q)^3-part by the explicit bottleneck lemma asserting triple vanishing of P_{d,r,n}(q) at primitive nth roots, then apply the abstract multiplicity-three criterion. Combine the two coprime divisibility statements to obtain divisibility of P_{d,r,n}(q) by the full modulus [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Finally, use the coprimality of the clearing denominator E_{d,n}(q) with the modulus to convert divisibility of P_{d,r,n}(q)=E_{d,n}(q)Δ_{d,r,n}(q) into the desired rational-function congruence Δ_{d,r,n}(q) ≡ 0 mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2, which is exactly the theorem.

steps.derives: From the theorem hypotheses n > 1 and n ≡ 1 mod 2d, conclude that n is odd and gcd(d,n)=1.
steps.trivial_justification: Write n = 1 + 2dt for some integer t. Then n is odd. If a positive integer c divides both d and n, then c also divides n - 2dt = 1, so c = 1. Hence gcd(d,n)=1.

steps.derives: Define E(q) = E_{d,n}(q) = (q^{2d};q^{2d})_{n-1}, define Δ(q) = Δ_{d,r,n}(q) = Σ_{k=0}^{n-1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k ((q^d;q^d)_k)^2 q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2}/(q^{2d};q^{2d})_k - [rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2}, define P(q) = P_{d,r,n}(q) = E(q)Δ(q), define U(q) = U_n(q) = ∏_{m|n, 1<m<n} Φ_m(q), and define M(q) = [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.
steps.trivial_justification: This step only introduces abbreviations for the common denominator, the theorem difference, the cleared difference, the proper-divisor cyclotomic factor, and the target modulus.

steps.derives: The cleared difference P(q) belongs to the Laurent polynomial ring Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Step A0 provides that n is odd, and Step A1 defines P(q) exactly as in Lemma L1. Therefore Lemma L1 applies directly and yields P(q) ∈ Z[q^{±1}].

steps.derives: For every divisor m of n with 1 < m < n and every primitive mth root of unity ξ, one has P(ξ)=0.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the conclusion of Lemma L5 for the P(q) defined in Step A1 under the theorem hypotheses.

steps.derives: The Laurent polynomial P(q) is divisible by U(q)=U_n(q) in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Step A2 shows that P(q) is a Laurent polynomial, and Step A3 shows that P(q) vanishes at every primitive mth root of unity for every proper divisor m of n. Lemma L4 converts exactly those vanishing conditions into divisibility by the product U_n(q) of the corresponding proper-divisor cyclotomic polynomials. Since Step A1 defined U(q)=U_n(q), the claimed divisibility follows.

steps.derives: For every primitive nth root of unity ζ, one has P(ζ)=0, P'(ζ)=0, and P''(ζ)=0.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the conclusion of Lemma L7 for the cleared difference P(q) defined in Step A1.

steps.derives: The Laurent polynomial P(q) is divisible by Φ_n(q)^3 in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Step A2 gives P(q) ∈ Z[q^{±1}], and Step A5 gives triple vanishing of P(q) at every primitive nth root of unity. Lemma L6 states that these hypotheses imply divisibility by Φ_n(q)^3, so Φ_n(q)^3 divides P(q).

steps.derives: One has M(q)=U(q)Φ_n(q)^3, and gcd(U(q), Φ_n(q)^3)=1 in Z[q].
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L3 gives [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2 = U_n(q) Φ_n(q)^3 and gcd(U_n(q), Φ_n(q))=1. Step A1 identifies U(q) with U_n(q) and M(q) with [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2, so the factorization M(q)=U(q)Φ_n(q)^3 follows immediately. Since gcd(U(q), Φ_n(q))=1, the same holds with Φ_n(q)^3 in place of Φ_n(q).

steps.derives: The Laurent polynomial P(q) is divisible by M(q)=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2 in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Step A4 shows U(q) divides P(q). Step A6 shows Φ_n(q)^3 divides P(q). Step A7 states that U(q) and Φ_n(q)^3 are coprime and that their product is exactly M(q). Applying Lemma L8 with A(q)=U(q), B(q)=Φ_n(q)^3, and L(q)=P(q) gives divisibility of P(q) by U(q)Φ_n(q)^3, which Step A7 identifies with M(q).

steps.derives: The polynomials E(q) and M(q) are coprime in Z[q].
steps.trivial_justification: Step A0 gives that n is odd and gcd(d,n)=1. Step A1 defines E(q)=E_{d,n}(q) and M(q)=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Lemma L2 applies under exactly those hypotheses and yields gcd(E(q), M(q))=1.

steps.derives: The polynomial M(q) has constant term 1, so M(0)=1.
steps.trivial_justification: Step A1 defines M(q)=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Because n>1, the q-integer [n]_q = 1+q+...+q^{n-1} has constant term 1, and the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_n(q) also has constant term 1. Therefore their product M(q) has constant term 1.

steps.derives: The rational function Δ(q)=Δ_{d,r,n}(q) satisfies Δ(q) ≡ 0 mod M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Step A1 gives the identity P(q)=E(q)Δ(q). Step A2 shows P(q) is a Laurent polynomial. Step A8 shows that M(q) divides P(q) in Z[q^{±1}]. Step A9 gives gcd(E(q),M(q))=1, and Step A10 gives M(0)=1. Therefore all hypotheses of Lemma L9 are satisfied with the present P(q), E(q), M(q), and Δ(q), and Lemma L9 yields Δ(q) ≡ 0 mod M(q).

Step A11 states that Δ(q) ≡ 0 mod M(q). Step A1 defines Δ(q) as exactly the displayed theorem difference and defines M(q)=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Substituting those definitions into the congruence from Step A11 gives the displayed zero-difference congruence.

steps.derives: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.
steps.trivial_justification: Step A12 says exactly that the difference between the finite sum and the right-hand side is congruent to 0 modulo [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. This is precisely equivalent to the displayed congruence between the finite sum and the right-hand side.
